text.p: Celebrations marking five years of Kazakh independence on Monday were overshadowed by poverty, ethnic frictions and a realisation the former Soviet republic is still beholden to Moscow for export of its oil riches.

Thousands braved the winter cold in the Kazakh capital Almaty, the tree-lined streets frosted white, to witness the unveiling of a "monument to independence", a bronze archer standing on a winged snow leopard.
Sky-blue flags have replaced the red Soviet hammer and sickle but the traditional costumes and dancers echoed the carefully orchestrated festivities of the Soviet past.
"We are still not fully conscious of this gift of fate," said Kazakh film director Sergei Azimov at the unveiling.
But around the monument, a large police presence showed government unease.
Independence has brought the majority of the Central Asian nation's 16.9 million population, scattered across a territory five times the size of France, only increased hardship.

On the same day 10 years ago, the Soviet authorities used fire engines to hose down hundreds of rioting students in sub-zero temperatures in Almaty. The protests were sparked by the appointment of an ethnic Russian as the republic's Communist Party boss but many say the underlying reason was poverty.

"This is no time for a celebration," said Lena, 30 and scraping a living like thousands of others by trading cheap goods. One of a large minority of ethnic Russians in the republic, she added: "It is not our celebration."
Salaries and pensions are low, if they are paid at all and many families cannot afford enough to eat. Shortages of electricity and gas are a potential killer.
"They (government) are afraid of a putsch," said Yuri, an ethnic Russian truck driver, repeating a widespread rumour on the number of police near the new monument.
Yuri, like many Russians in the republic, has felt sidelined by ethnic Kazakhs since independence. "People are hungry, angry, you can only push Russian Ivan so far."

A new language law under consideration, which would make the Kazakh language mandatory for all state jobs, is unlikely to ease their fears. Already, hundreds of thousands have left for Russia in the last five years.

Delivering an independence day speech in both Kazakh and Russian, Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev urged ethnic accord. "Here (Kazakhstan) there will never be disagreement between nationality or belief."
But the habitually cautious Kazakh leader made no bones about his nation's colonial past.
"The whole of Kazakh history has been its battle for independence...colonialism continued here after the (1917) revolution," he said.

He called for a minute's silence for the victims of Josef Stalin's forced collectivisation, the "basmachi" guerrilla bands who fought the Soviets and victims of the nuclear tests which poisoned vast areas of Kazakh territory.
Nazarbayev was at pains, however, to stress good relations with the republic's former colonial overlord for Kazakhstan still relies mostly on Russian pipelines for export of its huge oil wealth.
